title: Letters to kings
hookLine: letters go to Heraclius, the Persian king, the Negus and others

cards: Mud-brick houses. A mosque roofed with palm leaves. From this small town, Medina, riders set out with letters: to the emperor of Rome, the king of kings of Persia, the Christian king of Abyssinia, the ruler of Egypt.
Two of them rule the great empires of the day. It's a little like a small-town mayor writing personally to the heads of the world's great powers.
But somebody in Medina points out a problem: kings don't read letters unless they're sealed. So the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has a ring made.

teach.b: Sahih al-Bukhari describes the ring: silver, engraved with three words in three lines. Muhammad. Messenger.
God. The letters went out in the calm after Hudaybiyyah, when the roads were safe.

The one to the Roman emperor, kept in Bukhari, has this shape: in the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate; from Muhammad, the servant of God and his messenger, to the great one of his people; peace on whoever follows guidance.
Then an invitation to Islam, and a verse from the Qur'an calling the People of the Book to a word common between them: that we worship none but God.
The emperor, Heraclius, was in Jerusalem, and Bukhari keeps an account of what he did.

He called for anyone from Arabia who happened to be nearby, and found a trading caravan from Mecca, traveling because of the new peace, led by Abu Sufyan, still the Prophet's enemy. Heraclius questioned him closely.
Does this man lie? No. Does he break promises?
No. Who follows him, the powerful or the weak? The weak.
Abu Sufyan said later he wanted to lie, but was ashamed to be caught lying in front of his own men. The emperor treated the letter with respect, and in the end kept his throne and his faith.
The king of Persia tore his letter to pieces. The biographers say the Negus of Abyssinia received his kindly, and the ruler of Egypt sent back courteous words and gifts.
The letters were the same: honest, short, sealed, and sent.

how: Muslims read the letters and the Heraclius hadith, found in the opening book of Sahih al-Bukhari, as a model of respectful, direct invitation, and some Muslim men wear a ring on the little finger following the Prophet's seal ring.

o: the Persian king who tore the Prophet's letter up
the Meccan trader questioned about the Prophet
the Roman emperor who received the Prophet's letter

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: silver, three words in three lines

s: the ring was made because kings only read sealed letters
so the Prophet had a silver ring engraved: Muhammad, messenger, God.
Abu Sufyan praised the Prophet because he was already Muslim
he was still an enemy; he said he was ashamed to be caught lying.
every king answered the letters the same way
one tore it, some answered kindly, and the emperor kept his throne and faith.

games.q: you're Abu Sufyan, the Prophet's enemy, questioned by the emperor in front of your own men. he asks: does this man lie? what do you say?
o: yes, he lies all the time.
I don't know him well enough to say.
games.why: he told the truth: no. he said later he wanted to lie, but was ashamed to be caught in front of his men.

practice: Let someone come to mind you've been meaning to say something true to: a thank-you you never sent, an apology, a word of support.
Version it in your head, short, like the Prophet's letters: who it's from, who it's to, peace, and one honest thing. Don't decide yet whether you'll send it.

wordCard.voice: Heraclius, the Roman emperor who received one of the sealed letters the Prophet sent from Medina, and questioned a Meccan caravan leader closely about him.

orig.note: Arabic: Muhammad, messenger of God, the words engraved on the seal ring.

carryVoice: Your line: sealed and sent. Even to an emperor, a few true words. See you tomorrow.
